description: I am Rohan Bankapur. I like coding and space, and this is an intersection of both of my interests. I am just here to have fun and looking for people that can offer skillsets I don't have and is willing to join!
summary: Emberline is a web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into fire-safety answers for lunar habitats. NASA plans to run Moon habitats and pressurized rovers at 8.2 psia and 34% oxygen. Astronauts breathe that air normally, but fire responds to the oxygen fraction, and a NASA flame-spread model predicts flames there spread about 1.5 to 1.8 times faster than on the ISS. Emberline organizes all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics database, maps the oxygen levels each one tested, and ranks the experiments most relevant to a chosen habitat. It reveals a clear gap: no fabric or plastic burn test in the database goes above 22.1% oxygen. A built-in AI analyst answers plain-English questions using only NASA sources and checks every citation before showing it. Emberline gives habitat designers, researchers, and students a fast, honest starting point and shows NASA exactly where new fire experiments are needed.
details:
Emberline is a web dashboard that helps engineers, researchers, and students understand fire risk in crewed space habitats using NASA's microgravity combustion data. A user picks a habitat, such as the ISS, a lunar base, or the planned lunar habitat and rover atmosphere of 8.2 psia and 34% oxygen. Emberline then shows the oxygen range each of the 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database tested, ranks the experiments most relevant to that habitat, and estimates how much faster flames would spread there compared with ISS air. A searchable Experiments view lists every investigation with its fuels, test conditions, key findings, and DOIs, and lets users compare investigations side by side.

To build it, we parsed 13 PSI investigation pages and their metadata, 154 individual CFI-G test records, and published NASA reports into structured data with 30 cited findings. The relevance ranking is a transparent weighted score that users can inspect row by row. The flame-spread estimate uses a published NASA correlation (Olson et al., 2008) and is clearly labeled as an estimate with its valid range. Emberline also includes an AI analyst, powered by Gemini, that answers plain-English questions using only retrieved NASA passages. It follows two published research methods, In-Context Retrieval-Augmented Language Modeling and ALCE citation evaluation. Every sentence carries a citation, and the server rejects any citation to a passage it did not retrieve. On a 20-question test, the analyst cited an expected source 95% of the time with no unsupported sentences.

Emberline's main benefit is that it surfaces a gap otherwise buried in terabytes of data: no fabric or plastic burn test in PSI goes above 22.1% oxygen, yet lunar habitats are planned at 34%. This gives habitat designers a fast, traceable starting point and helps NASA prioritize the experiments still needed, such as the upcoming FM2 lunar flammability test. The project is creative because it goes beyond summarizing papers. It places every experiment on one map against real mission atmospheres and explains a counterintuitive result: crews breathe oxygen partial pressure, but fire responds to oxygen fraction, so air that is safe to breathe can still be more flammable.

We prioritized scientific honesty throughout. Values a source does not report stay marked "not reported" instead of being estimated, every number links to its source, and the interface keeps each screen simple and readable. The app also keeps working on free services, falling back to saved and extractive answers if the AI quota runs out. We built Emberline with TypeScript, React, Next.js, and Tailwind CSS, used Python and pandas for the data pipeline, the Gemini API for the analyst, and Vercel for hosting, and made the demo video with Playwright and FFmpeg.
